before: VALENTINE. With your permission, my lord, I was not admitted. But her handmaid returned this answer: For seven summers’ heat, no eye, not even the sky, shall behold her face fully revealed. Like a cloistered nun she will walk veiled, watering her chamber once a day with tears that sting the eyes — all this to preserve a dead brother’s love, which she means to keep fresh and lasting in her sorrowful remembrance.
after: VALENTINE. My lord, they wouldn’t let me in, but her maid gave me this answer. For seven summers even the sky won’t see her face unveiled. She’ll walk veiled like a nun and water her chamber every day with tears that sting her eyes. With all that salt she means to preserve her love for her dead brother and keep it fresh in her grieving memory.

before: CAPTAIN. By the same chance you yourself were saved.
after: CAPTAIN. It was chance that saved you, too.

before: MARIA. No — either tell me where you’ve been, or I won’t open my lips wide enough for a bristle to enter as an excuse for you. My lady will hang you for your absence.
after: MARIA. Either tell me where you’ve been or I won’t open my lips so much as a hair’s breadth to make excuses for you. My lady will have you hanged for staying away.

before: MALVOLIO. I marvel that your ladyship takes pleasure in such a sterile rascal. I saw him outdone the other day by an ordinary fool with no more brain than a stone. Look — he’s already out of ammunition. Unless you laugh and give him occasion, he’s muzzled. I declare, I rate these wise men who crow at such professional fools no better than the fools’ stooges.
after: MALVOLIO. I’m amazed that you enjoy such a witless rascal. The other day a common fool with no more brains than a stone got the better of him. Look, his guard is down already. Unless you laugh and give him an opening, he’s gagged. As for the wise men who crow over professional fools like these, I think they’re just the fools’ own clowns.

before: MALVOLIO. Not yet old enough for a man, nor young enough for a boy — like a squash before it’s a peapod, or an unripe apple just before it’s ripe. He’s caught between the tide — between boy and man. He is very handsome, and he speaks very saucily. One would think his mother’s milk was hardly out of him yet.
after: MALVOLIO. Not old enough to be a man, or young enough to be a boy. Like a young pea pod before it fills out, or an apple just short of ripe. He is in the slack water between boy and man. Very good-looking and very cheeky. You would think the milk was scarcely dry on his lips.

before: CLOWN. Would you like a love-song, or a song about good living?
after: CLOWN. Would you like a love song or a song about leading a virtuous life?

before: SIR ANDREW. Yes, yes. I don’t care for good living.
after: SIR ANDREW. Yes, yes, a love song. I don’t care for the virtuous life.

before: SIR ANDREW. If you love me, let’s do it. I’m a dab hand at a round.
after: SIR ANDREW. If you love me, let’s sing. I’m a regular hound at a catch!

before: CLOWN. By Our Lady, sir, some dogs can catch well.
after: CLOWN. By Our Lady, sir, some hounds can catch very well.

before: DUKE. Oh, fellow, come — the song we had last night. Mark it, Cesario — it is old and plain. The spinsters and the knitters in the sun, and the free maids who weave their thread with bone shuttles, are accustomed to chant it. It is simple truth, and toys with the innocence of love as in the old times.
after: DUKE. Come, fellow, the song from last night. Listen, Cesario. It’s old and simple. Women sing it as they spin and knit in the sun, and girls as they make lace with bone bobbins. It tells a simple truth and plays with the innocence of love, as in the old days.

before: MALVOLIO. It’s just fortune — everything is fortune. Maria once told me she fancied me, and I have heard her herself come this near to saying that, should she fancy anyone, it should be one of my complexion. Besides, she treats me with a more exalted respect than anyone else who serves her. What should I make of it?
after: MALVOLIO. It’s fortune. Everything is fortune. Maria once told me my lady was fond of me. And I’ve heard my lady herself come close to saying that if she took a fancy to anyone, it would be someone of my complexion. Besides, she treats me with much more respect than anyone else in her service. What am I to think?

before: SIR TOBY. Try out your legs, sir — put them in motion.
after: SIR TOBY. Taste your legs, sir. Put them in motion.

before: SIR TOBY. Go, write it in a martial hand. Be sharp and brief. It doesn’t matter how witty, so long as it’s eloquent and inventive. Taunt him with the license that ink permits. If you ‘thou’ him three times, it won’t be amiss. And as many lies as will fit in your sheet of paper — though the sheet were big enough for the great bed of Ware in England — set them down. Go to it. Let there be gall enough in your ink, even though you write with a goose-quill, no matter. About it.
after: SIR TOBY. Go, write it in a warlike hand. Be sharp and brief. Never mind how witty it is, so long as it’s eloquent and inventive. Give him all the insults your ink will allow. Call him ‘thou’ three times for good measure. Accuse him of lying as many times as you can fit on the sheet, even if it’s as big as the great bed of Ware in England. Get to it. Put plenty of gall in your ink, even if you do write with a goose quill. Off you go.

before: SIR TOBY. I have been precious to him, lad — to the tune of some two thousand strong, or so.
after: SIR TOBY. And I’ve cost him dear, lad. About two thousand, give or take.

before: ANTONIO. Perhaps your eye will fall on some trinket you want to buy. And your money, I think, is not for idle markets, sir.
after: ANTONIO. You may see some little thing you want to buy, and I doubt you have money to spare for shopping.

before: ANTONIO. Let me speak a little. This youth you see here, I snatched one half out of the jaws of death; relieved him with such sanctity of love; and to his image, which I thought promised most venerable worth, did I render devotion.
after: ANTONIO. Let me speak a moment. This young man you see here was halfway down the jaws of death when I pulled him out. I cared for him with a love that was sacred to me. I looked at him and saw such promise of worth that I worshipped him.

before: CLOWN. ‘Vent my folly’! He has heard that word from some great man, and now applies it to a fool. ‘Vent my folly’! I’m afraid this great lubber, the world, will prove a sissy. Now please, undo your strangeness, and tell me what I shall vent to my lady. Shall I vent to her that you are coming?
after: CLOWN. ‘Vent my folly’! He picked up that word from some great man and now tries it on a fool. ‘Vent my folly’! This great lout of a world will turn out to be a pampered city boy, I fear. Now put off those strange manners and tell me what I should vent to my lady. Shall I vent the news that you are coming?

before: MALVOLIO. They have treated me like a property. They keep me in darkness, send ministers to me, asses, and do all they can to drive me out of my wits.
after: MALVOLIO. They use me as a prop. They keep me in the dark, send clergymen to me, the asses, and do everything they can to make me think I’ve lost my mind.

before: [As Sir Topas.] Hold no words with him, good fellow. [As
after: [As Sir Topas.] Don’t speak to him, good fellow.

before: himself.] Who, I, sir? Not I, sir. God be with you, good Sir Topas. [As Sir Topas.] Indeed, amen. [As himself.] I will sir, I will.
after: [As himself.] Who, me, sir? No, sir. God be with you, good Sir Topas. [As Sir Topas.] Indeed, amen. [As himself.] I will, sir, I will.

before: FIRST OFFICER. Orsino, this is that Antonio who took the _Phoenix_ and her cargo from Candy. And this is he who boarded the _Tiger_ when your young nephew Titus lost his leg. Here in the streets, desperate with shame and station, in a private brawl we apprehended him.
after: FIRST OFFICER. Orsino, this is the Antonio who captured the Phoenix and her cargo from Crete. He boarded the Tiger when your young nephew Titus lost his leg. We caught him brawling in the streets here, heedless of his reputation or his position.

before: OLIVIA. Whatever it pleases my lord that shall become him.
after: OLIVIA. Whatever pleases you, my lord, so long as it becomes you.

before: DUKE. Oh you dissembling cub! What will you be when time has sown a gray on your hide? Or will not your craft so quickly grow that your own trip will be your overthrow? Farewell, and take her — but direct your feet where you and I henceforth may never meet.
after: DUKE. You deceitful cub! What will you be when your fur turns gray? Or will your cunning grow so fast that your own tricks trip you up? Farewell, take her. But go where you and I will never meet again.
